item.title: Comprehension Debt - the hidden cost of AI generated code. | AddyOsmani.com
item.author: Addy Osmani
item.description:
Comprehension Debt - the hidden cost of AI generated code. | AddyOsmani.com
2026-11-21
Por Addy Osmani
https://addyosmani.com/blog/comprehension-debt/
Comprehension Debt - the hidden cost of AI generated code.
March 14, 2026
Comprehension debt is the hidden cost to human intelligence and memory resulting from excessive reliance on AI and automation. For engineers, it applies most to agentic engineering.
There’s a cost that doesn’t show up in your velocity metrics when teams go deep on AI coding tools. Especially when its tedious to review all the code the AI generates. This cost accumulates steadily, and eventually it has to be paid - with interest. It’s called comprehension debt or cognitive debt.
Comprehension debt is the growing gap between how much code exists in your system and how much of it any human being genuinely understands.
Unlike technical debt, which announces itself through mounting friction - slow builds, tangled dependencies, the creeping dread every time you touch that one module - comprehension debt breeds false confidence. The codebase looks clean. The tests are green. The reckoning arrives quietly, usually at the worst possible moment.
Margaret-Anne Storey’s describes a student team that hit this wall in week seven: they could no longer make simple changes without breaking something unexpected. The real problem wasn’t messy code. It was that no one on the team could explain why design decisions had been made or how different parts of the system were supposed to work together. The theory of the system had evaporated.
That’s comprehension debt compounding in real time.
A recent Anthropic study titled “How AI Impacts Skill Formation” highlighted the potential downsides of over-reliance on AI coding assistants. In a randomized controlled trial with 52 software engineers learning a newlibrary, participants who used AI assistance completed the task in roughly the same time as the control group but scored 17% lower on a follow-up comprehension quiz (50% vs. 67%). The largest declines occurred in debugging, with smaller but still significant drops in conceptual understanding and code reading. The researchers emphasize that passive delegation (“just make it work”) impairs skill development far more than active, question-driven use of AI. The full paper is available arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20245.
There is a speed asymmetry problem here
AI generates code far faster than humans can evaluate it. That sounds obvious, but the implications are easy to underestimate.
When a developer on your team writes code, the human review process has always been a bottleneck - but a productive and educational one. Reading their PR forces comprehension. It surfaces hidden assumptions, catches design decisions that conflict with how the system was architected six months ago, and distributes knowledge about what the codebase actually does across the people responsible for maintaining it.
AI-generated code breaks that feedback loop. The volume is too high. The output is syntactically clean, often well-formatted, superficially correct - precisely the signals that historically triggered merge confidence. But surface correctness is not systemic correctness. The codebase looks healthy while comprehension quietly hollows out underneath it.
I read one engineer say that the bottleneck has always been a competent developer understanding the project. AI doesn’t change that constraint. It creates the illusion you’ve escaped it.
And the inversion is sharper than it looks. When code was expensive to produce, senior engineers could review faster than junior engineers could write. AI flips this: a junior engineer can now generate code faster than a senior engineer can critically audit it. The rate-limiting factor that kept review meaningful has been removed. What used to be a quality gate is now a throughput problem.
I love tests, but they aren’t a complete answer
The instinct to lean harder on deterministic verification -
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Chips suffer worst week since 2001 as the Nasdaq nears a bear market
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
Chips suffer worst week since 2001 as the Nasdaq nears a bear market
2026-11-21
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/chips-are-crashing-like-its-2008-as-the-nasdaq-100-nears-a-bear-market-192805534.html
Wall Street is wrapping up a kind of week it has seen only five other times since World War II. Two of them came in 2008 and 2001.
The S&P 500 (^GSPC) fell every day this week, with four drops of 1% or more. That had happened only in 1962, 1974, 1978, the week after the 9/11 attacks in 2001 and October 2008, according to Bespoke Investment Group.
Friday brought the sharpest leg down. The S&P 500 fell nearly 4% and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) more than 5%, wiping out the Nasdaq's gain for 2026. The S&P 500 shed about $2.4 trillion in market value on the day and closed in a correction, 10% below its Oct. 6 record, for the first time since April 2025. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) closed in one too.
The Nasdaq 100 (^NDX) finished just shy of a bear market, or a 20% drop from its record closing high. Meanwhile, chip stocks had their worst week since the one after the 9/11 attacks.
The strange part is the timing. This was supposed to be a showcase week for AI. Nvidia's (NVDA) first report since Jensen Huang's exit showed revenue more than doubling, and Anthropic (ANT) pulled off the biggest IPO ever. Both stocks sank anyway. Tech stocks that beat earnings forecasts this season fell an average of 1.5% on their report days, the worst reaction to good news since at least 2001, according to Bespoke.
Read more: How to protect your money during turmoil, stock market volatility
Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value since its Oct. 6 top, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. Broadcom (AVGO), Micron (MU) and AMD (AMD) each fell about 12% to 14% Friday alone. A Yahoo Finance basket of 62 chip stocks lost about $1.5 trillion on the day, and the reasons keep piling up, including a reported SEC probe of its accounting,.
Chips are reliving 2008
The PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) fell about 17% this week and has lost a third of its value since Sept. 30. That puts chips on track for their worst two months since late 2008, a pace topped only in the dot-com bust and the financial crisis. Chips hit their financial-crisis low 18 years ago to the day, on Nov. 20, 2008.
The Nasdaq 100 and the tech sector are on the same track. The S&P 500 is headed for its worst November since 1973, and the Nasdaq for its worst since 2000. The S&P 500 has given up about $8 trillion since its record, nearly $6 trillion of it this week.
The rest of the market isn't
That's where the 2008 comparison breaks down. In October and November 2008, the typical S&P 500 stock lost about 28%. This time, the equal-weight S&P 500 (RSP) is about flat since Sept. 30.

The PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) fell about 17% this week and has lost a third of its value since Sept. 30. That puts chips on track for their worst two months since late 2008, a pace topped only in the dot-com bust and the financial crisis. Chips hit their financial-crisis low 18 years ago to the day, on Nov. 20, 2008.
The Nasdaq 100 and the tech sector are on the same track. The S&P 500 is headed for its worst November since 1973, and the Nasdaq for its worst since 2000. The S&P 500 has given up about $8 trillion since its record, nearly $6 trillion of it this week.
The rest of the market isn't
That's where the 2008 comparison breaks down. In October and November 2008, the typical S&P 500 stock lost about 28%. This time, the equal-weight S&P 500 (RSP) is about flat since Sept. 30.

item.title: Nvidia drops 12%, Broadcom and AMD extend declines as the AI trade melts down
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
Nvidia drops 12%, Broadcom and AMD extend declines as the AI trade melts down
2026-11-21
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/nvidia-amd-and-broadcom-lead-chip-stocks-lower-133658985.html
Chip giant Nvidia (NVDA) extended its declines on Friday, dropping 12%. The stock headed for seven straight days of losses amid a reported SEC probe into the chip maker's accounting practices.
Shares of peers AMD (AMD) and Broadcom (AVGO) also tanked double-digit percentages as a broader AI trade sell-off intensified. Broadcom has significant financial ties to Anthropic (ANT), which made its public debut on Thursday. Under an arrangement disclosed in Anthropic's prospectus, the chipmaker agreed to lend the AI developer up to $42 billion to help finance its infrastructure build-out and purchase about $1 billion of Anthropic shares as part of its IPO-related private placement.
On Friday, Anthropic's stock fell as much as 12% amid a broader tech sell-off.
Memory chipmaker Micron Technology (MU) and peer SK Hynix (SKHY) dropped more than 10%. Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM) and equipment maker ASML (ASML) also declined.
Yorkville Ives' Dan Ives said the AI trade weakness "is a panic-driven sell-off" in tech "rather than a red flag moment indicating darker times ahead for tech and the market."
"Big Tech will be spending capex next year in the $1.5 trillion range, and that is not changing because of the panic in the market the last few months," he wrote on Friday.
The broader chip sector fell on Thursday following the public debut of AI model maker Anthropic. The sector was already on shaky ground following the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and concerns over AI financing.
Nvidia is down more than 22% year to date, putting it on pace for its first annual decline since 2022, when the Federal Reserve began a rate-hiking cycle, according to Yahoo Finance's AlphaSpace data.
Other areas of the AI trade were under pressure Friday, with optical equipment maker Coherent (COHR) and Bloom Energy (BE) stocks sinking 6% and 7%, respectively.
Neocloud providers CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius (NBIS) both extended losses from the prior session, declining roughly 9%.

item.title: Gap stock pops even as warm fall weather leads the retail giant to cut its forecast
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Gap stock pops even as warm fall weather leads the retail giant to cut its forecast
2026-11-21
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/gap-stock-pops-even-as-warm-fall-weather-leads-the-retail-giant-to-cut-its-forecast-130937620.html
The warm fall weather hasn't been kind to Gap (GAP). But investors don't seem to care.
Shares of the owner of Gap, Old Navy, Banana Republic, and Athleta rose 15% as investors shrugged off a mixed quarter and focused on improved sales at Old Navy and continued strength at Gap.
Third-quarter sales rose 2% to $4 billion, while comparable sales were flat. Adjusted earnings came in at $0.82 a share, topping estimates of $0.78.
Comparable sales at the Gap brand jumped 9%, marking 12 straight quarters of gains.
Old Navy comparable sales were flat, improving from a 4% drop in the second quarter as the company course-corrected on its assortments.
Banana Republic fell 3%, and Athleta continued to be a challenge, as seen in a 15% sales drop.
But warmer fall weather softened demand in October and early November, forcing Gap to slash its full-year sales outlook to roughly flat from prior guidance for 1% to 1.5% growth.
The company also cut its adjusted earnings forecast to $2.29 to $2.34 a share from $2.35 to $2.45.
"We view 3Q as mixed, with Gap Inc. delivering better-than-expected profitability and sequential improvement at Old Navy, while Gap brand momentum remained strong. However, softer October/early November demand drove lower FY26 sales and profit guidance, with added promotions weighing on 4Q GM. We see encouraging underlying progress, but holiday execution remains key," Jefferies analyst Corey Tarlowe said.

item.title: Anthropic's IPO winners and losers, from Ashton Kutcher to Sam Bankman-Fried
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
Anthropic's IPO winners and losers, from Ashton Kutcher to Sam Bankman-Fried
2026-11-21
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/anthropics-ipo-winners-and-losers-from-ashton-kutcher-to-sam-bankman-fried-110000728.html
Ashton Kutcher and Sam Bankman-Fried both bet early on Anthropic. Only one is celebrating its public market debut.
Bankman-Fried's FTX put $500 million into Anthropic (ANT) in 2021 for about 14% of the AI lab. After FTX collapsed, the estate sold the stake in 2024 for about $1.3 billion. Among the buyers was Jane Street, the trading firm where Bankman-Fried got his start.
That stake was worth more than $40 billion at Anthropic's first-day close of $97.17 — even after the stock opened at $111.50, 34% above its $83 IPO price, and gave back part of the pop. Bankman-Fried, who is serving a 25-year sentence, told the New York Times from prison that he tries not to dwell on it. "There's no point in obsessing over regrets," he said. "But it's certainly something that I've spent, despite that, a fair bit of time thinking through."
Kutcher, meanwhile, had a different response: "Kind of cool," the actor said of the IPO on X. Sound Ventures, the firm he co-founded with Madonna's manager Guy Oseary, first backed Anthropic in 2023. Its $435 million turned into about $6 billion by the close, with some outlets reporting that the debut could make Kutcher a billionaire, despite his recent exit from the firm. NBA star Tristan Thompson is another celebrity backer, and he isn't selling.
Everyone else got rich too
Anthropic's seven co-founders were worth about $163 billion combined at the close, or more than $23 billion apiece, by Yahoo Finance calculations. They were the only insiders selling in the IPO, at about $280 million each.
The seven have pledged to give away 80% of their stock. That's about $130 billion at the close, more than the Gates Foundation's entire $92 billion endowment. The filing calls the pledges "voluntary, revocable," and the seven keep 50.1% of the vote either way.
Employees did fine as well. Their options and restricted stock were worth about $270 billion at the close. The average option costs just $2.91 a share to exercise, on a stock that closed at $97.17.
Then there's Big Tech
Amazon (AMZN) has put in $18 billion, and its roughly 15% stake was worth $190 billion at the close. Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) owns about 14%, worth about $175 billion. Nvidia (NVDA) had the quickest payday, turning a $10 billion buy at the IPO price into a gain of about $1.7 billion by the close.
Anyone who chased the open came up short, down about 13% by the close. Pricing 980 million shares at $83 left nearly $14 billion on the table, just shy of SpaceX's record $14.4 billion in University of Florida professor Jay Ritter's data. Its bankers didn't, with Goldman Sachs (GS) and Morgan Stanley (MS) set to collect about $113 million each.

item.title: Consumer sentiment ticked up amid post-election optimism
item.author: Claire Boston
item.description:
Consumer sentiment ticked up amid post-election optimism
2026-11-21
Por Claire Boston
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/consumer-sentiment-ticked-up-amid-post-election-optimism-152954161.html
Consumer sentiment ticked higher in November as consumers grew more confident about short-term and long-term business conditions following the election.
The University of Michigan's Consumer Sentiment Index rose 7.3% to 51.5 in November, from October's reading of 48. Economists expected a similarly sized improvement to 51.6.
There's evidence that consumers' economic views have shifted after Democrats' massive gains in the Nov. 6 midterm elections. November's survey was conducted between Oct. 20 and Nov. 16, and expectations surged among independent voters, a group that largely moved left this cycle. Expectations also improved for Democrats, and fell among Republicans.
"Consumers appear to anticipate potential changes to public policy under a divided government to come," Joanne Hsu, the survey's director, said in a statement.
Read more: How to protect your money during turmoil, stock market volatility
Lower-wealth consumers saw their personal finances improve the most last month, helped by lower gas prices. But those with the most stock holdings said their personal finances deteriorated, likely due to recent market fluctuations stemming from AI jitters.
Americans' inflation expectations for the year ahead improved markedly this month, falling to 3.7% from 4.7% in October. Still, the numbers remain higher than the 3.4% consumers expected in February, before the Iran War began.
While the numbers improved this month, elevated inflation, high gas prices, and the potential for an artificial intelligence bubble are still leaving consumers feeling gloomy about the economy.
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

item.title: The biggest myth about American immigration policy
item.author: Matthew Yglesias
item.description:
The biggest myth about American immigration policy
2026-11-21
Por Matthew Yglesias
https://www.slowboring.com/p/the-biggest-myth-about-american-immigration
For a while now I’ve been wanting to write about a widespread misunderstanding about the history of American immigration policy. Fortunately, Donald Trump’s decision to respond to the blue wave by promoting Stephen Miller to chief of staff gives us a news hook, because he is a frequent purveyor of this misunderstanding.
This is from an April profile of Miller in the New York Times, and even though the authors quibble with Miller, they actually miss his biggest mistake:
Mr. Miller has blamed many of the country’s problems on a landmark 1965 law that paved the way for more Hispanic and Asian immigrants, a shift from primarily allowing in Europeans.
Despite decades of data showing that immigrants outperform native-born Americans on major indicators, including crime rates and use of welfare, Mr. Miller contends that those who entered after the 1965 law, as well as their descendants, have largely been unsuccessful.
“If you bring those societies into our country and then give them unlimited free welfare, what do we think’s going to happen?” he told Fox News in December. “We need a moratorium on immigration from third world countries until we can heal ourselves as a nation.”
Here’s the issue: While it is true that the United States enacted a major change in immigration policy in 1965 and it is also true that Hispanic immigration to the United States increased significantly after 1965, it’s simply not the case that the 1965 law paved the way for more Hispanic immigrants. It’s actually the complete opposite — the 1965 law imposed quantitative restrictions on immigration from Latin America that didn’t exist previously.
It would probably be going too far to say that it’s a total coincidence that these things changed at around the same time, but the relationship is indirect and unrelated to the text of the immigration law.
What Hart-Celler did
The law at issue is the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, also known as the Hart-Celler Act after its main authors.
This law was a major reversal of immigration policy from the National Origins Formula adopted back in 1921. These 1921 immigration quotas were not adopted to keep out people from the “third world” as Miller would understand it. The point of the 1921 law was to prevent people from Southern and Eastern Europe — people like Miller’s ancestors or First Lady Melania Trump — from coming to the United States.
It also restricted immigration from Asia, though Asian immigration was already severely limited by laws such as the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 and the 1907 “Gentlemen’s Agreement” with the Japanese government to stop giving passports to U.S.-bound Japanese laborers. The Naturalization Act of 1870 made it impossible for immigrants from Asia to become American citizens while for the first time explicitly creating a process of naturalization for “aliens of African nativity and to persons of African descent.”
Which is just to say that this was all happening under a very different political paradigm than the contemporary immigration debate.
You often hear restrictionists express nostalgia for the midcentury immigration system. But they’re really just saying they liked the low level of immigration — or maybe that they approve of the broad principle of discriminating on the basis of nationality — not that we should replicate the specific details of the quota system. Nobody today thinks the United States should prefer immigrants from Western Europe over immigrants from Eastern Europe.
At any rate, the impetus for the Hart-Celler Act was to create a non-discriminatory immigration system in which your ability to get a visa would be based on individual-level criteria rather than nation of origin.
But in the case of Latin America and the Caribbean, that meant making policy more restrictive.

This is from an April profile of Miller in the New York Times, and even though the authors quibble with Miller, they actually miss his biggest mistake:

Mr. Miller has blamed many of the country’s problems on a landmark 1965 law that paved the way for more Hispanic and Asian immigrants, a shift from primarily allowing in Europeans.

Despite decades of data showing that immigrants outperform native-born Americans on major indicators, including crime rates and use of welfare, Mr. Miller contends that those who entered after the 1965 law, as well as their descendants, have largely been unsuccessful.

“If you bring those societies into our country and then give them unlimited free welfare, what do we think’s going to happen?” he told Fox News in December. “We need a moratorium on immigration from third world countries until we can heal ourselves as a nation.”

Here’s the issue: While it is true that the United States enacted a major change in immigration policy in 1965 and it is also true that Hispanic immigration to the United States increased significantly after 1965, it’s simply not the case that the 1965 law paved the way for more Hispanic immigrants. It’s actually the complete opposite — the 1965 law imposed quantitative restrictions on immigration from Latin America that didn’t exist previously.

It would probably be going too far to say that it’s a total coincidence that these things changed at around the same time, but the relationship is indirect and unrelated to the text of the immigration law.

What Hart-Celler did

The law at issue is the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, also known as the Hart-Celler Act after its main authors.

This law was a major reversal of immigration policy from the National Origins Formula adopted back in 1921. These 1921 immigration quotas were not adopted to keep out people from the “third world” as Miller would understand it. The point of the 1921 law was to prevent people from Southern and Eastern Europe — people like Miller’s ancestors or First Lady Melania Trump — from coming to the United States.

It also restricted immigration from Asia, though Asian immigration was already severely limited by laws such as the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 and the 1907 “Gentlemen’s Agreement” with the Japanese government to stop giving passports to U.S.-bound Japanese laborers. The Naturalization Act of 1870 made it impossible for immigrants from Asia to become American citizens while for the first time explicitly creating a process of naturalization for “aliens of African nativity and to persons of African descent.”

Which is just to say that this was all happening under a very different political paradigm than the contemporary immigration debate.

You often hear restrictionists express nostalgia for the midcentury immigration system. But they’re really just saying they liked the low level of immigration — or maybe that they approve of the broad principle of discriminating on the basis of nationality — not that we should replicate the specific details of the quota system. Nobody today thinks the United States should prefer immigrants from Western Europe over immigrants from Eastern Europe.

At any rate, the impetus for the Hart-Celler Act was to create a non-discriminatory immigration system in which your ability to get a visa would be based on individual-level criteria rather than nation of origin.

item.title: Morning Brief: People treated Anthropic way differently than SpaceX
item.author: Newsletter
item.description:
Morning Brief: People treated Anthropic way differently than SpaceX
2026-11-20
Por Newsletter
Plus: Kalshi hired its GTA researcher after 33,000 applications.
Friday, November 20 |
View in your browser
Good morning!
Anthropic's stock skyrocketed after the opening bell Thursday morning,
opening 34% above its IPO price
and cresting the $111 mark before closing at $97 per share.
After the $81 billion raise, the biggest IPO ever,
we finally know what the company is "worth
." At the close, Anthropic held a market-tested valuation of $1.27 trillion, answering the huge question we've all wanted to know.
Congratulations to Anthropic.
But not to the stock market. Despite that frenzy, markets had a rough day, with the S&P 500 (
^GSPC
) falling 1.4%, the Nasdaq (
^IXIC
) 1.5%, and the Dow (
^DJI
) 1.7% as the
tech trade continued to falter
We would say one can only imagine how big Anthropic would be if it had picked a different moment. But given previous estimates pegging the company at up to $2 trillion, we do have some idea of what it might be worth if 2026's boom times boomerang back.
In today's issue
Anthropic's IPO ties the fate of the US economy closer to AI
Retail investors are treating Anthropic much differently than SpaceX
Kalshi hired its GTA researcher after 33,000 applications
Roaring Kitty posts, and GameStop roars
What we're watching Friday:
Anthropic's first
full
day of trading on Friday will still be the main thing we're watching as the hype and FOMO fade and reality sets in.
A light day on the calendar centers on consumer sentiment readings from the University of Michigan.
Yahoo Finance Morning Brief is written by
Ethan Wolff-Mann
and
Hamza Shaban
Headlines
Cyberattacks continue as
JPMorgan, Visa, and Mastercard disclose cyberattack on vendors.
Why token usage could become a key metric
for AI investors amid the Anthropic IPO.
Micron president warns memory supply constraints
will be even 'tighter.'
Walmart beats Q3 earnings expectations,
raises 2026 outlook again
Palo Alto Networks CEO has a theory
on the outages hitting major US companies
How Anthropic retail trading compares to SpaceX's
IPO.
Market snapshot
Key market moves from last session
Powered by
See the bigger picture.
Anthropic's IPO ties the fate of the US economy closer to AI
Digital billboards advertise Anthropic on the day of its IPO in Times Square, New York, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)
The day finally arrived. Anthropic (
ANT
) began trading on Thursday at $111.50 per share, surging above its $83 IPO price and briefly attaining a market capitalization of $2 trillion before settling into a still-respectable market cap of $1.2 trillion. What took years for the tech giants to achieve,
the frontier AI lab grabbed in an instant
But
the historic IPO is notable not just for its size
, but for what it says — and will say — about the makeup of the stock market and the outsized influence of its largest players.
The top 10 biggest companies make up close to 40% of the S&P 500. A bad day for tech means a bad day for the market. And now that
Anthropic has joined the trillion-dollar ticker club
— though it won’t join the S&P 500 (
^GSPC
) anytime soon — Wall Street's fate is tightly bound to another huge tech company which also happens to be an AI lab without a long track record of financial stability.
The top-heavy nature of the S&P 500 means the benchmark index is less diverse than it looks. Sure, investors are buying into a basket of hundreds of names. But since the tickers with the largest market caps get the highest proportional weights, a handful of names can move the entire index.
That's how you can get such different performances from the equal- weighted S&P 500 (
^SPXEW
) index (up 11% so far this year) versus the standard, market-weighted version (up 6%).
Big Tech's importance in the stock market has attracted praise and concern for years, even before the arrival of Ch

item.title: The cat came back: Roaring Kitty tweet sends GameStop stock higher amid GTA VI fervor
item.author: Paige Oamek
item.description:
The cat came back: Roaring Kitty tweet sends GameStop stock higher amid GTA VI fervor
2026-11-20
Por Paige Oamek
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/the-cat-came-back-roaring-kitty-tweet-sends-gamestop-stock-higher-amid-gta-vi-fervor-184220345.html
Influential investor Keith Gill, also known as Roaring Kitty, has returned, and GameStop (GME) shares are rising after the meme stock trader who made millions betting on the company returned to the discourse as gamers everywhere celebrated the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI."
After being MIA online for nearly two years, at 11:30 a.m. ET on Thursday, Roaring Kitty tested the waters with a mysterious post on X: a photo of "Cat Mario."
GameStop stock popped roughly 3% immediately following his tweet.
Gill's post lands at a dizzying moment for markets, just roughly an hour after Anthropic's (ANT) IPO went live and on the day Take-Two (TTWO) launched GTA VI.
Read more live reviews, memes, and updates from the 'GTA 6' release
Yesterday, GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen said publishers are making a mistake by releasing games as digital downloads instead of physical discs. "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," Cohen told Bloomberg.
GameStop's stock is up more than 30% since the beginning of the year, buoyed by its eBay (EBAY) stake and interest.
The image is of Mario wearing a cat power-up in "Super Mario 3D World." It's not clear what Roaring Kitty's Mario post means — if anything at all — but the market is reacting and powering up the stock.

item.title: Walmart, Costco see some panic-buying after tech outages
item.author: Brooke DiPalma
item.description:
Walmart, Costco see some panic-buying after tech outages
2026-11-20
Por Brooke DiPalma
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/walmart-costco-see-some-panic-buying-after-tech-outages-191922568.html
A wave of tech outages and disruptions affecting Apple (AAPL), Chase (JPM), Microsoft (MSFT), and US airlines has sent consumers spiraling over the past week, prompting people to stock up on emergency supplies.
"We have seen a small amount of that," Walmart (WMT) CFO John David Rainey told Yahoo Finance (see video above). "Certainly categories like jug bottled water or propane are selling at higher comps with that concern, but it's really relatively small to our overall business. It's worth noting that oftentimes when we see that, it's a pull forward of future demand."
Read more: Here are all of the major national disruptions in November
Rainey said the company will stick to its outlook despite a minimal sales lift. On Thursday, Walmart raised its full-year outlook for the third time this year. It now expects net sales to increase by 4.9% to 5.2%, up from 4% to 5%.
Walmart isn't alone in seeing panic buying amid consumer anxieties that a cyberattack or other outage could lead to more catastrophic system failures. Wholesale retailer Costco (COST) is also seeing a boost, according to Mizuho analyst David Bellinger.
"Consumer anxiety, following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media, have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," he wrote in a note to clients.
As of Nov. 15, he said 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators online were sold out.
"These one-time lifts, combined with pantry-loading and a value connotation into the holiday period, all add to an already very elevated valuation for shares," Bellinger said, who raised his price target on Costco stock to $1,150 from $1,110.
Shoppers stockpiling emergency supplies led to an increase in same-store sales growth at US Costco stores, not including fuel purchases. Sales increased 11% to 12% in the final week of October, Bellinger wrote, adding that the bump continued in the first two weeks of November.
Search "doomsday food" on the Costco app, and shoppers will find that emergency food supplies from ReadyWise, Ready Project, and Chef's Banquet are all sold out.
Yahoo Finance also reached out to Target (TGT) about whether it's seeing any panic buying, but the retailer said it has nothing to share at the moment.
Follow Brooke DiPalma on X at @BrookeDiPalma or email her at bdipalma@yahoofinance.com.

Shoppers stockpiling emergency supplies led to an increase in same-store sales growth at US Costco stores, not including fuel purchases. Sales increased 11% to 12% in the final week of October, Bellinger wrote, adding that the bump continued in the first two weeks of November.
Search "doomsday food" on the Costco app, and shoppers will find that emergency food supplies from ReadyWise, Ready Project, and Chef's Banquet are all sold out.
Yahoo Finance also reached out to Target (TGT) about whether it's seeing any panic buying, but the retailer said it has nothing to share at the moment.
Follow Brooke DiPalma on X at @BrookeDiPalma or email her at bdipalma@yahoofinance.com.

item.title: Anthropic IPO: 3 weird facts to know before you buy the stock
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Anthropic IPO: 3 weird facts to know before you buy the stock
2026-11-20
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/anthropic-ipo-3-weird-facts-to-know-before-you-buy-the-stock-130027579.html
If you are eyeing a purchase of Anthropic's (ANT) stock on its IPO day today or in the coming days, you will have to accept that this isn't exactly a normal public company.
Seven somewhat strange founders control all the shots at Anthropic, for one. And two, there is basically a competitor in OpenAI's (OPAI.PVT) ChatGPT doing the same thing as Anthropic.
But if you dig deeper into Anthropic's business, there are more interesting factoids you will also have to get comfortable with if you want to be a shareholder.
- Anthropic has a donation-matching program in which employees can pledge a meaningful portion of their equity awards or the equivalent cash proceeds to a donor-advised fund or other nonprofit organization, and the company then matches those donations with shares of its Class N common stock. The company incurred $2.1 billion in expenses in the first nine months of 2026 related to this program, representing about 6% of total operating expenses. It saw $541 million in these expenses in 2025.
- Water is a legitimate risk to Anthropic's ability to grow its business quickly. "Our facilities separately depend on access to reliable water for cooling, which in some regions is scarce, subject to use restrictions, or increasingly costly. Any of the foregoing could adversely affect the availability of the power or water we require, increase our costs, or limit our ability to develop, expand, or operate our data center facilities, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations," the company noted in its S-1 filing.
- Anthropic may have to pay for compute whether or not it uses it. The company noted in its S-1 filing, "Our equipment supply framework agreements and similar arrangements may expose us to further risks, including minimum purchase or take-or-pay commitments, price escalation, and obligations that we are unable to align with our actual deployment needs."
The market debut is shaping up to be big for Anthropic despite its many quirks. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, valuing the Claude maker at $1.5 trillion.
Follow live updates of Anthropic's IPO here.
The company priced its shares at $83 each, above its initial range of $70 to $78. It will debut on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT".
While the IPO saw strong demand, it does come with an asterisk: The earnings results haven't been great.
In an amended S-1 filing, Anthropic said that third quarter sales rose 1,127% to $17 billion. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-over-quarter basis. Third quarter sales increased 47% compared with a 144% growth rate in the second quarter. Sales increased 132% in the first quarter.

item.title: Stalemates over semiconductors and rare earth minerals appear little changed as Trump heads home from China
item.author: Ben Werschkul
item.description:
Stalemates over semiconductors and rare earth minerals appear little changed as Trump heads home from China
2026-11-20
Por Ben Werschkul
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/stalemates-over-semiconductors-and-rare-earth-minerals-appear-little-changed-as-trump-heads-home-from-china-121555352.html
Stalemates over semiconductors and rare earth minerals appear little changed as Trump heads home from China
Meetings between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping ended Thursday with little change in ongoing economic standoffs over semiconductors, rare earth minerals, and tariffs, even as both leaders made outsized displays of personal affection.
"We have a very special relationship, and I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we will never have a problem," Trump told Xi, who began the visit in Shenzhen by hugging Trump after he landed Wednesday.
But the leaders actively sidestepped difficult topics on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting.
At one point, they ignored a question about Jensen Huang and Nvidia (NVDA) and whether the ousted CEO was "loyal to the United States." China then barred that Bloomberg correspondent from the next photo-op, according to reporters at the event.
Trump even seemed to acknowledge the low expectations as he sat across from Xi Thursday.
"A lot of people weren't sure would something come out of the meetings," he said. "I think something will come out very, very strongly," as he ticked through ongoing economic issues as well as the conflicts in the Middle East and in Ukraine.
The dynamic was similar when Russian President Vladimir Putin joined the conversation at Kylin Villa, a Chinese government compound in Shenzhen, for meetings that Trump said focused on Ukraine.
Trump called the Russian leader his "friend," but there was little evidence of any progress over the war. Ukraine sent a clear message during the gathering by attacking an important bridge that connects Russia and Crimea for the third night in a row.
Trump arrived back at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport after 6 p.m. local time on Thursday for the long flight back to Washington.
Trade truce set to end in January
The meeting began with low expectations of advancing trade issues and ended with no apparent agreement to extend a truce that has lowered tariffs between the US and China that expires on Jan. 10.
The meeting centered on a new "Board of Trade" that aims to strike a 30-for-30 tariff framework to lower tariffs on roughly $30 billion in annual imports from each country.
Xi talked about the need for world leaders to "abandon Cold War thinking" and avoid "decoupling and supply chain disruptions" in language that seemed directed at the United States.
The comments appear to refer to new limits on semiconductor exports that the US proposed this week, which have already had a disruptive effect in Asia, as well as to China's limits on rare earth minerals, which have continued to frustrate the United States.

item.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explains why he asked 60K employees to quit
item.author: Julie Bort
item.description:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explains why he asked 60K employees to quit
2026-11-20
Por Julie Bort
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/microsoft-ceo-satya-nadella-explains-004256847.html
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff.
Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He's not saying he's replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He's saying he's reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI.
The buyout was "to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices," he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit.
"Let's take software engineering. We went from, 'Well, we don't buy that AI can ever do software.' To suddenly, 'Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?' To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point," he explained.
For some people, "that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?" he added, "but, I mean, it has to be done."
He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. "They build a software factory that builds the product. They don't build the product."
He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. "That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs."
But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn't grow up as an AI-first company. "So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?" he said. "It's going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, 'Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.'"
When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nadella further explained, "We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don't have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution."
He called out talk about the singularity (the hypothetical point at which AI surpasses human intelligence) and predictions that AI will take away all jobs. "All of that leads anyone who even wants to change to be sort of anxious … You have to sort of walk the hard walk of really making the structural changes, getting people slotted, giving them opportunity."
In other words, the buyout was the message to employees: You can get with the new AI-first program, which will radically change your job, or you choose to get on with your life. Elsewhere.

item.title: Traders Are Betting on Interest Rates Staying High for Years
item.author: James Hirai
item.description:
Traders Are Betting on Interest Rates Staying High for Years
2026-11-20
Por James Hirai
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/traders-betting-interest-rates-staying-135251721.html
(Bloomberg) -- Traders are betting that major central banks will keep interest rates largely unchanged for years once they've finished hiking at the end of 2027.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Money markets began 2026 pricing in rate cuts by the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of England but had to pivot when the Iran war throttled oil supplies, lifting inflation. Traders flipped to betting on a series of hikes, while also wagering that easing would follow next year.
Those hopes for lower borrowing costs have almost vanished as the conflict drags on and a wave of investment in technology, rearmament and the energy transition boosts competition for funding, fueling higher bond yields. All three central banks are expected to raise rates further in the next 12 months, and then mostly sit tight at least until 2031, based on interest rate futures.
"I call this the yield era," said Bob Stoutjesdijk, investment strategy and portfolio manager at Osmosis Investment Management. "We are living in a world of structurally higher rates of inflation."
Companies went on a borrowing binge to finance investment in artificial intelligence this year, hitting the market with a record flood of bonds and hoovering up hundreds of billions of dollars. There's much more debt to come in 2027, according to JPMorgan Chase & Co., which sees big tech spending, and elevated refinancing needs, driving another record year of US investment-grade bond issuance.
Many Fed policymakers view the AI buildout as a material source of inflation risk, according to minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee's October meeting published this week.
In addition, governments are ratcheting up spending on defense and infrastructure, most notably in Germany, which is set to be the largest gross issuer of debt among euro area peers next year, according to strategists at Commerzbank AG.
Uncertain World
To be sure, oil prices have retreated from a six-month peak in recent weeks, but inflation numbers are still hot, fueling wagers on more rate hikes against a volatile geopolitical backdrop.
"Macro and political uncertainty remain elevated," said Christoph Rieger, head of rates and credit research at Commerzbank.

Those hopes for lower borrowing costs have almost vanished as the conflict drags on and a wave of investment in technology, rearmament and the energy transition boosts competition for funding, fueling higher bond yields. All three central banks are expected to raise rates further in the next 12 months, and then mostly sit tight at least until 2031, based on interest rate futures.
"I call this the yield era," said Bob Stoutjesdijk, investment strategy and portfolio manager at Osmosis Investment Management. "We are living in a world of structurally higher rates of inflation."
Companies went on a borrowing binge to finance investment in artificial intelligence this year, hitting the market with a record flood of bonds and hoovering up hundreds of billions of dollars. There's much more debt to come in 2027, according to JPMorgan Chase & Co., which sees big tech spending, and elevated refinancing needs, driving another record year of US investment-grade bond issuance.
Many Fed policymakers view the AI buildout as a material source of inflation risk, according to minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee's October meeting published this week.
In addition, governments are ratcheting up spending on defense and infrastructure, most notably in Germany, which is set to be the largest gross issuer of debt among euro area peers next year, according to strategists at Commerzbank AG.
Uncertain World
To be sure, oil prices have retreated from a six-month peak in recent weeks, but inflation numbers are still hot, fueling wagers on more rate hikes against a volatile geopolitical backdrop.
"Macro and political uncertainty remain elevated," said Christoph Rieger, head of rates and credit research at Commerzbank.

item.title: Anthropic IPO sets retail trading record as market sell-off weighs on buying
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
Anthropic IPO sets retail trading record as market sell-off weighs on buying
2026-11-20
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/retail-traders-pile-into-anthropic-ipo-but-net-buying-lags-spacex-212350846.html
Anthropic's (ANT) stock churned out more retail trading activity on its public debut than any other stock in its listing day going back to 2012, according to full Thursday trading data from Vanda Research.
The firm's data shows everyday investors traded $772 million worth of Anthropic shares, exceeding the $669 million recorded during SpaceX's (SPCX) first trading session in June and setting a record in Vanda's data, which goes back to 2012.
However, everyday investors were far less aggressive net buyers of shares through the day compared to SpaceX's blockbuster June listing. Net retail purchases totaled just $60 million or roughly half the $118 million that retail investors poured into SpaceX on its first day and a third less than the $92 million in Coinbase Global's (COIN) April 2021 debut, according to Vanda.
"Retail are turning up to trade Anthropic ... but not in the way that much of the street, ourselves included, had probably anticipated," Vanda Research analyst Viraj Patel wrote, noting that the share of retail buyers steadily declined across early trading.
Read more: How does Anthropic make money? Inside the business of AI.
Among the major reasons for the lower net buying, Patel cited "broader risk aversion in global markets" as major stock indexes fell Thursday. Smaller investors also may appear to be favoring an alternative to traditional stock trading, specifically the use of a crypto-related derivative product known as perpetual futures, which are tied to the price of the stock, Patel added.
The divergence suggests that retail investors were actively buying and selling Anthropic shares rather than accumulating them as aggressively as they did SpaceX. The net buying was also far below Vanda's estimate made ahead of the listing based on perpetual futures pricing.
The broader selloff came as retail investors have sold single stocks to fund their Anthropic purchases, rotating out of AI names like AMD (AMD) as buying in Nvidia (NVDA) stalled. Shares of AMD and Nvidia dropped 7% and 2%, respectively, in afternoon trading.
The final word on retail enthusiasm for the stock is still far from out, according to Patel. SpaceX's first-day net buying accounted for just 29% of its total in the first week, according to the company.
Story has been updated with end of day data.

item.title: Walmart beats Q3 earnings expectations, raises full-year outlook again
item.author: Brooke DiPalma
item.description:
Walmart beats Q3 earnings expectations, raises full-year outlook again
2026-11-20
Por Brooke DiPalma
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/walmart-beats-q3-earnings-expectations-raises-full-year-outlook-again-184415236.html
Walmart's (WMT) third quarter earnings came in ahead of expectations, and the retail giant raised its outlook for fiscal 2027 as e-commerce sales surged.
America's biggest retailer, often considered a bellwether for the industry and a key pulse check for what the holiday season could look like, posted revenue of $188.8 billion, just above the $187.2 billion expected, according to Bloomberg consensus data. Adjusted earnings per share clocked in at $0.65, a cent higher than expectations.
US same-store sales growth moderated to 2.9% year over year, as analysts forecast. E-commerce sales grew 17% globally and 23% in the US.
CEO John Furner said the company "delivered strong results" and its core business is "gaining market share." He added that growth is coming from several parts of Walmart's business model, including "membership and agentic shopping."
Walmart raised its 2026 outlook for the third time this year. It now expects net sales to increase by 4.9% to 5.2%, up from 4% to 5%.
Operating income is expected to be in the 8% to 8.6% range, above the previously expected 7% to 8.5% range. Adjusted earnings outlook is also expected to be in the range of $2.84 to $2.89, above the previous range of $2.80 to $2.87.
Furner told investors on the call that Walmart can now reach 96% of US households in less than 3 hours, and 60% in less than 30 minutes.
"We have a unique ability to get closer to customers, use inventory more effectively, and deliver with speed at a low relative cost. Over 80% of e-commerce orders in the US are fulfilled from stores, including our marketplace orders," he added.
During the quarter, Walmart's US advertising business grew 37%. The company also introduced a subscription bundle that combines Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus for $120 per year, plus tax.
Sam's Club's same-store sales grew 9.7% as Americans turned to the wholesale retailer for fuel, grocery items, and general merchandise.
Walmart US CEO David Guggina said that the Walmart+ membership base grew in the double digits following the launch of its bundle option, and members increased their online spending with Walmart by more than 80% compared to before the launch. He added that customers with a membership spend four times as much as non-members.
Grocery sales also increased in the mid-single digits in the quarter as shoppers focused on essentials while also seeking out holiday items. The company posted some of the highest gains in groceries in three years.
Walmart cut prices on almost 8,000 products at its stores in the quarter. Furner said the company is doing all it can to keep prices as low as possible, despite pressure from higher fuel costs.

item.title: Memory supply constraints will be even 'tighter' in 2027: Micron CTO
item.author: Paige Oamek
item.description:
Memory supply constraints will be even 'tighter' in 2027: Micron CTO
2026-11-20
Por Paige Oamek
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/article/memory-supply-constraints-will-be-even-tighter-in-2027-micron-cto-173141999.html
Laptops are getting more expensive, and chipmakers are feeling the squeeze. The culprit? The ongoing memory shortage that's been plaguing the sector.
Unfortunately, it doesn't look like relief will arrive anytime soon, according to Micron (MU) president and CTO Scott DeBoer. In a recent interview on Deirdre Bosa Live (video above), he said supply and demand for memory won't line up for a long while.
"Our supply, we don't see it coming into balance anytime we can actually pick in the future right now," DeBoer said. The Micron president reiterated that 2027 is expected to be "tighter than 2026."
During fellow chipmaker Nvidia's (NVDA) Tuesday fiscal 2027 Q3 earnings call, its interim CEO Colette Kress noted that rising memory costs will cut into its margins.
As chipmakers race to build powerful AI systems, they need far more memory — especially DRAM — and Micron has been a beneficiary of this ever-climbing demand. DeBoer pointed to AI agents, which "are driving a significant amount of compute demand, memory demand," and that growth shows no signs of slowing.
Micron is investing over $250 billion in the US to expand DRAM capacity, along with expansions at existing fabs worldwide, but that kind of capacity takes "a long time to build, and that's a big part of the supply story that we're working to mitigate," DeBoer said.
Micron' stock is up roughly 145% since the beginning of the year.

item.title: JPMorgan, Visa, and Mastercard disclose cyberattack on third-party vendors
item.author: David Hollerith
item.description:
JPMorgan, Visa, and Mastercard disclose cyberattack on third-party vendors
2026-11-20
Por David Hollerith
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/jpmorgan-visa-and-mastercard-disclose-cyberattack-on-third-party-vendors-190314490.html
JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Visa (V), and Mastercard (MA) said on Thursday that some select customer data, including names and emails, was accessed by attackers after a cyberattack on a vendor.
Spokespeople for the companies said no payments or card data was leaked and that their own systems were not affected by the incident.
JPMorgan said it believes hackers who attacked a third-party vendor accessed marketing data, including customer names and email addresses. The bank also said the incident isn't related to outages many of its customers reported earlier this week, which it blamed on a software bug.
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," a JPMorgan spokesperson said.
"We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," a Mastercard spokesperson said. "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," the person added.
A Visa spokesperson added claims of the incident are associated to a third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region.
"This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week," the Visa spokesperson added.
A ransomware group known as n0n has claimed responsibility for the attacks on the dark web and shared sample data as proof, according to cybersecurity firm SOCRadar.
The cybersecurity firm told Yahoo Finance that it hasn't independently verified whether the ransomware group carried out the intrusion. It also supported JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard's statements that the breaches most likely originated at a third-party vendor and involved marketing and benefit-program data such as names and email addresses.
"The most immediate risk for consumers is targeted phishing that impersonates their bank or card provider," SOCRadar chief information security officer Ensar Seker said in an emailed statement.
The latest incident comes as consumers are on high alert after a string of major technology outages this November. The Wall Street Journal earlier reported the connection between the breaches and the ransomware group.
Follow David Hollerith on X @DsHollers.
Follow Brooke DiPalma on X at @BrookeDiPalma or email her at bdipalma@yahoofinance.com.

item.title: Nvidia, Broadcom, and Micron stocks decline as Anthropic goes public
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
Nvidia, Broadcom, and Micron stocks decline as Anthropic goes public
2026-11-20
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/nvidia-broadcom-micron-stocks-decline-as-anthropic-goes-public-170845481.html
Chip giant Nvidia (NVDA) stock slid into the red on Thursday, along with Broadcom (AVGO) shares, after Anthropic began trading. Intel (INTC) stock pared gains, closing up more than 1%.
Meanwhile, shares of chipmaker AMD (AMD) sank 7% after Hunterbrook Media disclosed a short position in the stock, citing questions about whether the company's semiconductors continued to reach a US-blacklisted Chinese server maker through intermediary companies despite export restrictions.
Memory chipmaker Micron Technology (MU) also lost gains as did peer SK Hynix (SKHY), dropping more than 2%.
Micron president and chief technology officer Scott DeBoer reiterated on Deirdre Bosa Live on Wednesday that memory supply in 2027 will be tighter than in 2026.
"Our supply, we don't see it coming into balance with demand really in any time we can actually pick in the future right now," he said.
The broader chip sector fell on Thursday following recent volatility, as the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and concerns over AI financing have created jitters across the AI trade.
Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM) and equipment maker ASML (ASML) erased earlier gains Thursday, leading the Technology (XLK) sector lower.
Other areas of the AI trade also trimmed gains on Thursday, with optical equipment maker Coherent (COHR) trimming gains. Bloom Energy (BE) shares declined modestly. Neocloud providers CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius (NBIS) both erased gains to close down 6% and 9% respectively for the session.
"Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Yorkville Ives' Dan Ives said on Wednesday evening.
The analyst noted that the AI trade is going through "a very turbulent, white-knuckle period that does not change our longer-term view that $3 trillion to $4 trillion of capex will be spent over the next few years."
The frontier lab's IPO "sets the stage for the next phase of tech and infrastructure investment, with Anthropic a central player in the buildout," Ives added.

https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/nvidia-broadcom-micron-stocks-decline-as-anthropic-goes-public-170845481.html

Chip giant Nvidia (NVDA) stock slid into the red on Thursday, along with Broadcom (AVGO) shares, after Anthropic began trading. Intel (INTC) stock pared gains, closing up more than 1%.

item.title: AMD stock drops after Hunterbrook Media raises export control concerns
item.author: Daniel Howley
item.description:
AMD stock drops after Hunterbrook Media raises export control concerns
2026-11-19
Por Daniel Howley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/amd-stock-drops-after-hunterbrook-media-raises-export-control-concerns-171508145.html
AMD (AMD) stock plunged more than 8% on Thursday after Hunterbrook Media published an investigation raising questions about potential export-control issues related to the chipmaker's products.
Hunterbrook Media is associated with Hunterbrook Capital, which has a short position on AMD.
According to the outlet, Chinese server maker IEIT continued to receive firmware updates for AMD's chips, despite being blacklisted by the US Department of Commerce.
Hunterbrook also claims three companies associated with IEIT, but not blacklisted, used software virtually identical to the firmware used by IEIT.
AMD, however, refuted Hunterbrook's claims in a statement to Yahoo Finance.
"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," a company spokesperson wrote.
"AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."
AMD rival Nvidia (NVDA) has also faced scrutiny over former CEO Jensen Huang's alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy and over concerns that customers circumvented export controls by shipping chips to China.
Huang resigned from Nvidia late last week and was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress.
AMD is viewed as a potential beneficiary of Nvidia's stumbles.
The company's stock is up more than 110% over the past 12 months, while Nvidia shares are down as much as 18%.
The AI trade has faced a number of headwinds recently as investors question the stability of the AI build-out and whether the boom will continue at its current pace.

item.title: Una propiedad para el futuro de tus hijos — pontblanc
item.author: Francisco Verdu A; Arquitecto MArch
item.description:
Una propiedad para el futuro de tus hijos — pontblanc
2026-11-19
Por Francisco Verdu A; Arquitecto MArch
https://www.pontblanc.eu/news-briefs/g3608yiz9iuaol8g0w3415euyqvf17-wp536-g52h4-5z74h-bhn2e-zz9p2-3hap7-pr4ha-pregj-azwrn-mjgcp-fkedh-86hee-wgrp6-n9rks
Fecha: 18 de noviembre de 2026, 16:43 h CET (Madrid)
La tranquilidad de hacer algo hoy por el futuro de tus hijos
Cuando todo cambia tan deprisa, da tranquilidad saber que has hecho algo concreto por el futuro de tus hijos. Que, vivan donde vivan, tengan una base en Madrid y algo propio sobre lo que construir.
Hace unos años asesoré a una familia de Chile en la compra de un piso junto a la Castellana: un piso precioso, fachada noble, tres balcones y mucha luz. Desde el principio decidimos que la vivienda estuviera a nombre de sus tres hijos, todos residentes fuera de España.
Los padres eligieron la propiedad conmigo y actuaron mediante poderes otorgados por sus hijos. Organizarlo llevó algo más tiempo, pero permitió dejar la titularidad definida desde la compra.
Hoy, los tres hijos tienen una parte de su patrimonio en Madrid, valorada en euros y en el contexto seguro y estable de la Unión Europea. Esta semana volvimos a hablar para afinar su estrategia de alquiler.
Esta semana miro el mercado, las dificultades de acceso de los jóvenes y una exposición que recuerda por qué también importa el entorno cultural en el que crecen las familias.
Pensar en el futuro no es solo acumular patrimonio: es darle una estructura y un propósito.
The Latest from Pontblanc
La Selección Pontblanc reúne viviendas con una ubicación excepcional y una arquitectura exquisita. Elegidas por el disfrute que ofrecen hoy y por el valor que protegen para el futuro.
Clave Privada de Acceso: PB2026
Top 3 noticias
1. Menos compraventas no significan mejores precios
Detalles clave
Las compraventas de viviendas inscritas en septiembre descendieron un 13,4 % interanual, según los datos provisionales publicados por el INE el 17 de noviembre [1]. El registro recoge operaciones escrituradas con anterioridad, por lo que no mide exactamente la actividad del mes.
Implicaciones
Para una compra familiar a largo plazo, una desaceleración general no basta para concluir que los precios van a bajar. Compararía el precio solicitado con operaciones cerradas (Portal de Notarios), la calidad del edificio y las posibilidades de uso de los hijos dentro de diez o veinte años.
2. La dificultad de comprar cambia las decisiones de los jóvenes
Detalles clave
Un análisis publicado el 16 de noviembre aborda cómo la dificultad para acceder a la vivienda lleva a algunos jóvenes a asumir inversiones financieras de alto riesgo con la esperanza de reunir el capital necesario para comprar [2]. Es una señal de presión sobre las expectativas de acceso, no una recomendación de inversión.
Implicaciones
Tener capacidad para pagar una cuota hipotecaria no significa disponer del ahorro inicial y de los gastos de adquisición. Si una familia quiere ayudar a sus hijos, estudiaría con tiempo si conviene comprar directamente a su nombre, aportar capital o conservar la titularidad de los padres: las consecuencias fiscales, legales y de control son distintas.
3. El Prado conecta poesía y pintura española
Detalles clave
El Museo del Prado presenta desde el 17 de noviembre una exposición sobre Rilke y el arte español, coincidiendo con el centenario de la muerte del poeta [3]. La propuesta explora el diálogo entre literatura y pintura.
Implicaciones
Una casa en Madrid puede ser también una puerta de entrada a una vida cultural compartida entre generaciones. Al elegir ubicación, me importa tanto la arquitectura del inmueble como lo que la familia podrá hacer y descubrir a pocos pasos de casa.
Construir Riqueza
Mercado inmobiliario y asignación de capital
Asignación de capital: Antes de iniciar la búsqueda, definiría el objetivo: uso familiar, alquiler, diversificación en euros o futura residencia de los hijos. Solo después deci
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: PANW Stock Surges 8% Overnight: Palo Alto Networks CEO Sees ‘Hundreds Of Billions Of Dollars’ Opportunity In Open-Weight AI Models Security
item.author: StockTwits Inc; Shivani Kumaresan
item.description:
PANW Stock Surges 8% Overnight: Palo Alto Networks CEO Sees ‘Hundreds Of Billions Of Dollars’ Opportunity In Open-Weight AI Models Security
2026-11-19
Por StockTwits Inc; Shivani Kumaresan
https://stocktwits.com/news-articles/markets/equity/panw-stock-palo-alto-networks-ceo-open-weight-ai-security-applied-compute/cNbLCSDR9ik
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Palo Alto Networks (PANW) stock jumped 8% overnight after a third-quarter (Q3) earnings beat, as CEO Nikesh Arora highlighted a market worth billions for securing open-weight AI models. Speaking on the Q3 earnings call, Arora outlined the company's Applied Compute acquisition, which aims to expand enterprise AI security and bring in $1 billion in annual recurring revenue by fiscal 2029.
Palo Alto Networks’ stock is on track for a second straight weekly gain.
Arora said during the Q3 earnings call that businesses are opting for AI models that give them greater ownership and control over their technology. Open-weight models have gained traction, making up more than 60% of token usage, compared with less than 5% a year earlier.
“When organizations put AI at the center of their operations, they want to retain control of their proprietary data, institutional judgment and competitive edge inside their own 4 walls. We expect a future with a serving opportunity in the hundreds of billions of dollars when enterprise applications are driven by open weight and open source adoption.”
To address the enormous security opportunity, Arora said Palo Alto Networks examined potential partners across the AI industry before selecting Applied Compute, citing its engineering capabilities and experience in developing open-weight models through post-training. Palo Alto Networks agreed to acquire Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion.
The Palo Alto-Applied Compute deal will focus on two things. Networks plans to integrate AI into its existing cybersecurity products, developing more than 35 specialized applications that will help customers counter AI-led threats with AI-driven defenses.
The second focus will be developing and delivering secure, sovereign versions of open-weight models for enterprise customers. “To support our efforts, we plan to build out a diversified global influence capability of north of 100-plus megawatts over the next 3 to 5 years,” Arora said.
“This will be supported by a modest CapEx commitment at least – of less than $3 billion through fiscal 2030, representing approximately half a year of our annual free cash flow.”
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock improved to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ territory. The stock recorded an 884% surge in message volume over the past 24 hours.
A user said, “Applied Compute acquisition to bolster PANW’s enterprise capabilities in open-weight AI models.”
Another user said, “$PANW agreed to pay $4.5B in stock for Applied Compute, which helps companies customize and run AI models. That’s a pretty big bet that the folks who buy their cybersecurity will also trust them to help run the models. I’d like to see how many customers sign up for both.”
PANW stock has gained 84% year-to-date.
Read Next: Why Did DIS, TGT, ASO Stocks Surge To 52-Week Highs Today?
For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com.
Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages.

item.title: A diversified investment strategy is not just prudent – it is essential
item.author: Texto propio
item.description:
A diversified investment strategy is not just prudent – it is essential
2026-11-19
Por Texto propio
A diversified investment strategy is not just prudent – it is essential
By Elias Nechachby
A year ago investors were bracing themselves for a year of uncertainty, upheaval and market volatility driven by conflicts, elections and other economic challenges around the world. Twelve months later, as we look to 2025, the picture is even more challenging.
While global rallies have benefited the equity markets around the world, valuations are now richer, and risks are bubbling under the surface.
Investors interested in shoring up their portfolios are likely attentive to the increased geopolitical risks following the new US presidency, and escalations of war across Russia and the Middle East.
The VIX Index, one of the most popular measures of expected stock market volatility, has had several big spikes in 2024 and is expected to continue to surprise investors in 2025. So, finding a way to manage expected market volatility will be critical for securing robust returns – and peace of mind.
Geopolitical, trade and economic risks
Looking forward, the febrile geopolitical, trade and economic backdrop points to greater volatility. And with some stock valuations over-extended, any upset could lead to a sizeable correction and in the worst case to a hard landing.
For example, the prospect of the US imposing import tariffs on goods from Canada, Mexico and China – its three biggest trading partners apart from the EU – would have ramifications for global businesses and their supply chains. It would also likely have inflationary, currency and other economic repercussions, all of which could have other unforeseen and unwelcome consequences.
So, finding a way to manage expected market volatility will be critical for securing robust returns – and peace of mind.
Confronted with that challenge, investors need to look carefully at their investment strategy to try and insulate their portfolio – after all, robustness is not achieved by chance.
Engineering investment learnings
Diversification is more often than not depicted as the diversification of assets, countries, sectors or stocks to insulate your portfolio against risk.
However, this type of diversification is insufficient as it only works in mild local market corrections, and does not work during global crises such as the 2008 global financial crisis (GFC) or 2020 Covid-19 pandemic.
As a starting point, to insulate their portfolio against potential risks, even though they may not be apparent in the short to medium term, investors need to look beyond the classic asset classes, sector, and country diversification, which notoriously fail to provide investors with any kind of protection during a severe crisis, when all correlations jump to one.
The traditional 60/40 stocks and bonds investment strategy saw a disastrous 2022, declining 17 per cent, with both asset classes seeing downward swings.
As an ex-aeronautical engineer, I approach risk in terms of ‘independent redundancy’. What I mean here is that an investment strategy needs to have several ‘engines’ that allow it to navigate different types of markets, and generate performance whether the market is up, down or flat.
Each ‘engine’ should be truly independent, or else there is an increased risk that they will all fail to perform at the same time. In aeronautics, you have to prove that the likelihood of undetected error for any critical system (that is, ‘the integrity’) is less than one in a billion. To reduce the probability of error and to reach that figure, one must have enough built-in independent redundancies.
That is why investors should look to diversify sources of alpha. Spreading investments across independent performance engines reduces exposure to concentrated risks, and benefit from varying growth opportunities and market dynamics, particularly as US trade policies, tax regulations, and global geopolitical shifts add
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Palo Alto Networks CEO just dropped a truth bomb on the network outages sweeping through major companies
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Palo Alto Networks CEO just dropped a truth bomb on the network outages sweeping through major companies
2026-11-19
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/palo-alto-networks-ceo-just-dropped-a-truth-bomb-on-the-network-outages-sweeping-through-major-companies-101129581.html
Palo Alto Networks CEO just dropped a truth bomb on the network outages sweeping through major companies
A cybersecurity CEO offers plain talk on the outages sweeping through major companies and disrupting everything from your email to your flight.
"I want to be clear, there are two distinct parallel effects that are driving this environment. The first effect is a massive surge in vulnerabilities and patches being deployed. We're seeing critical and severe vulnerabilities discovered nearly seven times the monthly average of last year. These discoveries are happening at a speed and intensity which is hard for IT teams to cope with," Palo Alto Networks (PANW) CEO Nikesh Arora said on his earnings call Wednesday evening.
Added Arora, "We believe many of the major disruptions of the last few weeks, including outages across major enterprises and governments, were partially due to unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes, as IT teams simply cannot patch these vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising their production environments. The second effect is the rise of AI-assisted cyberattacks. Bad actors are using open-weight models and new agentic frameworks to find and exploit vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed and scale. New agentic frameworks like ARTEX are enabling bad actors to turn simple instructions into autonomous, multi-stage attacks, allowing a handful of operators to compromise dozens of targets simultaneously. As we look ahead, we anticipate an elevated threat environment."
Something is breaking across corporate America — and the timing is getting harder to ignore.
United Airlines (UAL) suffered a system outage that delayed departing flights. JPMorgan Chase (JPM) experienced a software bug that slowed transactions and caused knock-on problems for customers at other banks, including Bank of America (BAC).
Just days earlier, an FAA network failure grounded flights nationwide for more than four hours. Microsoft's (MSFT) Outlook outage last week disrupted businesses around the world.
These incidents appear unrelated, and there is no evidence of a coordinated cyberattack. But when airlines, banks, and critical government systems all stumble within days of each other, it raises questions about critical infrastructure's vulnerability amid the push to advance AI.
The backdrop continues to be fertile ground for a cybersecurity player like Palo Alto Networks (PANW).
Revenue and operating profit for the most recent quarter surged 39% and 47%, respectively, from the year-ago period. Guidance for the current quarter and full year was also ahead of consensus estimates.
